rate-limiter.intro: A strong design makes the policy explicit, enforces it near the request path, and chooses a clear consistency tradeoff.

sections.title: Requirements and API
sections.body: Support per-API-key and per-endpoint limits, a configurable time window, and a clear 429 response with Retry-After. Clarify whether a short burst is allowed and whether limits are global or regional.

sections.title: Algorithm and storage
sections.body: Use a token bucket for a simple burst allowance and steady refill. Keep bucket state keyed by API key and policy. A fast in-memory or Redis-backed counter works at moderate scale; partition keys to spread hot traffic.

sections.title: Multi-region behavior
sections.body: For strict global quotas, route each key to a home region or use a coordinated shared store, accepting extra latency. If approximate limits are acceptable, allocate regional token budgets and reconcile asynchronously.

sections.title: Failure handling and operations
sections.body: Decide whether a limiter outage fails open or closed by endpoint risk. Protect the backing store with timeouts and local fallback limits. Track allowed and rejected requests, store latency, hot keys, and policy changes.

steps.name: Counter store
steps.detail: Atomically refills and consumes a token

stack.name: Envoy + Go
stack.reason: Envoy calls a Go rate limit service before forwarding protected requests.
stack.tradeoff: The extra RPC needs a short timeout and an explicit failure policy.

stack.reason: A Lua script refills and consumes the tokens in one operation on the shard that owns the key.
stack.tradeoff: A hot key can saturate one shard. Asynchronous replica failover can lose recent counts, so use a stronger store if the quota must be exact through failover.

url-shortener.intro: Separate the write path that creates short codes from the latency-sensitive redirect path.

sections.title: API and data model
sections.body: POST /links creates a record containing code, destination, owner, and expiry. GET /{code} returns a redirect. Use a unique index on code and a collision-safe ID generator such as a sequence encoded in base62 or random codes with retry.

sections.title: Redirect path
sections.body: Check a CDN or regional cache first, then a replicated key-value store. Cache popular redirects with bounded TTL and invalidate on deletion or destination changes.

sections.title: Scale and correctness
sections.body: Estimate redirects far exceed writes. Partition by code hash, replicate for reads, and keep code generation independent from the redirect database where practical. Define behavior for expired, missing, and malicious links.

sections.title: Operations
sections.body: Add rate limits, phishing detection, abuse reporting, and click analytics through an asynchronous event stream so analytics do not slow redirects.

stack.reason: Cache high traffic destinations near readers with a bounded TTL.

notification-service.intro: Model delivery as a durable workflow with per-channel queues, idempotency, and explicit provider feedback.

sections.title: Request and preferences
sections.body: Accept an idempotent notification request, resolve user preferences and consent, then create a durable notification record with channel, priority, and delivery state.

sections.title: Queues and workers
sections.body: Partition queues by recipient or tenant. Workers pull jobs and call email, push, or SMS providers with per-provider concurrency and rate limits. Retry transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter; dead-letter permanent failures.

sections.title: Delivery semantics
sections.body: Exactly-once delivery across external providers is generally unavailable. Use idempotency keys where supported, record attempts, and make duplicate delivery tolerable.

sections.title: Visibility and resilience
sections.body: Track queue age, provider success, retry counts, and end-to-end delivery time. Isolate provider outages and allow priority traffic to continue.

news-feed.intro: Choose a feed strategy based on the balance between write amplification and read latency, then make ranking and freshness explicit.

sections.title: Read and write paths
sections.body: For ordinary accounts, fan out new posts to follower inboxes on write for fast reads. For celebrity accounts, avoid massive write fan-out and merge their posts during reads.

sections.title: Feed storage
sections.body: Store ordered post IDs per user with timestamps and ranking metadata. Hydrate post details in batches from a cache and durable post store.

sections.title: Ranking and pagination
sections.body: Rank candidates using recency and product signals, and paginate with a stable cursor rather than offsets. Refresh asynchronously and provide a fallback when ranking is slow.

sections.title: Scale and quality
sections.body: Partition inboxes by user, cache the first page, and cap feed fan-out work. Monitor freshness, latency, duplicate rate, and engagement quality.

stack.reason: Consumers can replay publication events and retry inbox writes after outages.

stack.reason: Partition by reader and query the most recent entries by a timestamp and post ID sort key.
stack.tradeoff: Large accounts create write amplification. Merge their posts at read time instead of copying them to every inbox.

file-storage.intro: Keep file bytes in durable object storage and metadata in a transactional service, connected by a versioned sync protocol.

sections.title: Upload and storage
sections.body: Split large files into chunks, upload chunks with resumable IDs, then commit a manifest after integrity checks. Store immutable chunks in object storage and metadata separately.

sections.title: Sync and versioning
sections.body: Track a version vector or monotonically increasing revision per file. Devices request changes since their last revision; concurrent edits create explicit conflict copies or use a merge policy suited to file type.

sections.title: Sharing and security
sections.body: Represent access with ACLs or scoped share tokens. Check permissions on every metadata and download request, support revocation, and encrypt data in transit and at rest.

sections.title: Reliability
sections.body: Use checksums, replication, lifecycle policies, and restore tests. Monitor upload completion, sync lag, integrity errors, and storage costs.

stack.name: Amazon S3
stack.reason: Upload directly with multipart sessions and verify checksums before publishing a manifest.
stack.tradeoff: An uploaded object and a database commit are separate operations. Expire unattached uploads and reconcile gaps.

stack.name: MySQL (InnoDB)
stack.reason: Commit the current file version, part manifest, and change record in one transaction.
stack.tradeoff: An ordering scheme for sync cursors must handle concurrent commits. Segment the feed by account to contain contention.

metrics-platform.intro: Build a high-throughput ingestion path, control cardinality, and optimize storage for time-range queries and retention.

sections.title: Ingestion
sections.body: Agents batch and compress points, then publish to a partitioned stream. Validate schemas and apply backpressure or sampling when tenants exceed quotas.

sections.title: Storage and queries
sections.body: Partition by metric and time, organize data into time blocks, and use columnar compression. Keep recent data at high resolution and downsample older ranges.

sections.title: Cardinality and isolation
sections.body: Enforce label limits and identify expensive series before they overwhelm indexes. Separate tenant quotas and query budgets.

sections.title: Alerts and operations
sections.body: Evaluate alert rules close to the data, deduplicate notifications, and monitor ingestion lag, query latency, dropped points, and storage growth.

stack.name: OpenTelemetry Collector
stack.reason: Accept OTLP metric batches and apply bounded queues, resource labels, and ingress controls.
stack.tradeoff: More buffering absorbs bursts but adds lag, and labels still need cardinality limits.

stack.name: Apache Kafka
stack.reason: Buffer compressed batches by tenant and series identity for replay and backpressure.
stack.tradeoff: Replay can duplicate points. Decide how the storage writer handles repeated samples.

stack.name: ClickHouse
stack.reason: Store compressed metric columns in MergeTree tables and materialize common time buckets.
stack.tradeoff: High label cardinality and excessive small inserts increase memory and merge costs.

job-scheduler.intro: Separate durable schedule definitions from execution attempts, and make workers safe to retry after partial failure.

sections.title: Schedule storage
sections.body: Store each job’s next due time, recurrence rule, payload, and state. Partition due jobs by time bucket and shard so schedulers can scan bounded ranges.

sections.title: Claim and dispatch
sections.body: Schedulers atomically lease due jobs, enqueue execution records, and advance the next occurrence. Workers use lease expiry so abandoned jobs can be retried after crashes.

sections.title: Delivery guarantees
sections.body: At-least-once execution is practical; make handlers idempotent with job IDs. Retry transient errors with backoff and route exhausted jobs to a dead-letter state.

sections.title: Scale and correctness
sections.body: Use UTC timestamps, define recurrence and daylight-saving semantics, spread bursts with jitter, and track scheduling lag, retries, duplicate claims, and worker saturation.

stack.reason: Use visibility timeouts for abandoned work and a dead-letter queue for exhausted retries.
stack.tradeoff: Queue delivery is at least once. Workers still need a stable run ID and an idempotent side effect.

sections.title: Core architecture

sections.title: Data, scale, and tradeoffs

Make transcoding idempotent by video and rendition, retry failed jobs, and expose processing state to creators.

A trip service owns the authoritative state machine from requested to accepted, picked-up, completed, or cancelled. Use idempotency keys for requests and payments; tolerate slightly stale locations but prevent double assignment with conditional state transitions.

sections.title: Core architecture

Workers lease batches, honor robots rules and per-host concurrency limits, then fetch with strict time and size limits. Parsing extracts links and content into durable queues. URL and content fingerprints prevent repeated work. Indexing is a downstream pipeline. Use leases for crash recovery, exponential backoff for failures, and metrics for frontier age, host errors, and duplicate rates.

webhook-platform.intro: Drive the discussion from requirements and a rough capacity estimate to a durable asynchronous pipeline. State that a delivery may be repeated: exactly-once effects cannot be guaranteed when an external endpoint can receive a request but its acknowledgement is lost. Give each delivery a stable ID so receivers can deduplicate.

sections.title: Requirements, API, and capacity
sections.body: Assume 1B events/day: 1B ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11.6K events/s on average; design for 10× peaks, or about 116K events/s. With five destinations per event, expect 5B delivery attempts/day, about 58K/s average and 580K/s at peak before retries. At 1 KB/event, ingest is roughly 1 TB/day raw. Keep these estimates explicit and revise them if the interviewer changes fan-out or payload size. Offer POST /v1/events with tenant auth and an idempotency key; endpoint and subscription CRUD; GET /v1/deliveries/{id}; and an administrative replay endpoint.

sections.title: Data model and high-level design
sections.body: Store Tenant, Endpoint (URL, secret reference, status, concurrency policy), Subscription (tenant, endpoint, event type), immutable Event (event ID, tenant, type, payload, created time), Delivery (stable delivery ID, endpoint, event ID, state, next attempt), and DeliveryAttempt (status code, latency, timestamp). The ingest API validates and deduplicates, then writes the event and an outbox record transactionally. A publisher moves outbox entries into a partitioned durable log. Fan-out consumers resolve subscriptions and enqueue one delivery per endpoint into queues partitioned by endpoint or endpoint shard. Workers fetch payloads, sign each request with HMAC and a timestamp, and send with tight connect/read timeouts. Status updates and attempt records go to a queryable store.

sections.title: Retries, isolation, and ordering
sections.body: Retry timeouts, 429s, and selected 5xx responses with exponential backoff and jitter until the 72-hour deadline; do not retry permanent 4xx responses such as an invalid signature. Move exhausted deliveries to a dead-letter state and expose replay controls. Use per-tenant quotas, fair scheduling, and per-endpoint concurrency limits so a slow receiver cannot block others. If ordering is required for an endpoint, partition and serialize that endpoint’s queue; otherwise allow parallel delivery for throughput. At-least-once delivery can produce duplicates, so send an immutable delivery ID and require idempotent consumers.

sections.title: Security, operations, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Require HTTPS, validate endpoint ownership at registration, block private and link-local address ranges to reduce SSRF risk, and recheck DNS/redirect destinations. Keep signing secrets in a secret manager and support rotation. Encrypt stored payloads, apply tenant-scoped access checks, and set retention limits. Track queue age, delivery latency and success by tenant, retry rate, dead-letter count, and worker saturation; alert on growing oldest-message age. Partitioning by endpoint preserves local ordering and fair throttling but creates hot partitions; shard oversized endpoints and relax order only when the contract allows. Keep the event log durable, scale consumers horizontally, and make outbox publishing and state transitions idempotent.

payment-processing.intro: Treat the payment lifecycle as a durable state machine backed by an immutable ledger. Make idempotency explicit at both the merchant API and the provider boundary. A timeout is an unknown outcome, not proof that the provider did nothing.

sections.title: Requirements, API, and scale
sections.body: Clarify whether the first version supports authorization and later capture, immediate capture, refunds, and multiple currencies. Offer POST /v1/payment-intents with a merchant idempotency key, POST /v1/payment-intents/{id}/confirm, POST /v1/payment-intents/{id}/capture, POST /v1/refunds, and GET /v1/payment-intents/{id}. At 50M attempts/day, average load is about 580/s; size the write path for the stated 10K/s peak. At 2 KB per request/event, ingress is roughly 20 MB/s at peak before replication and callbacks.

sections.title: Data model and high-level design
sections.body: Store PaymentIntent (merchant, amount, currency, state, version), IdempotencyRecord (merchant, key, request hash, response), ProviderAttempt (provider reference, attempt number, outcome), LedgerTransaction and immutable LedgerEntry rows, plus ReconciliationRecord. The API gateway authenticates merchant requests. An orchestration service validates amounts and transitions the intent with a conditional version update. In one database transaction it stores the state and an outbox event. A publisher puts the event on a durable queue; provider workers tokenize payment details and call an acquirer using a stable provider idempotency key. Signed provider callbacks enter a separate callback API, are deduplicated, and advance the state machine. The ledger service records balanced debit/credit entries atomically when an authorization, capture, refund, or settlement is recognized.

sections.title: Correctness under retries and timeouts
sections.body: A unique constraint on (merchant_id, idempotency_key) returns the original result for a repeated request; reject reuse with a different request hash. Process queue messages and callbacks idempotently using stable event IDs. If a provider request times out after submission, mark the attempt outcome unknown, query the provider by its idempotency/reference key, and wait for callbacks or reconciliation before issuing another charge. Do not claim exactly-once effects across the provider boundary. Model explicit states such as requires_confirmation, processing, authorized, captured, declined, refund_pending, and refunded; allow only legal conditional transitions.

sections.title: Security, availability, and reconciliation
sections.body: Use a token vault so card numbers do not enter ordinary service logs or databases; encrypt sensitive tokens and scope access. Verify callback signatures and timestamps. Partition intents and ledger queries by merchant/account, but keep each ledger transaction atomic. Apply provider-specific timeouts, circuit breakers, and bounded retry with jitter. A scheduled reconciliation job compares provider settlement reports with internal attempts and ledger entries, records discrepancies, and routes them for repair without mutating the audit trail. Monitor unknown outcomes, duplicate requests, callback lag, authorization rate, reconciliation gaps, and queue age. Prefer returning a pending state over risking a duplicate charge during an outage.

feature-flag-platform.intro: Separate configuration authoring from evaluation. Keep evaluations in the client or regional data plane, and distribute immutable, versioned configuration snapshots. Define the freshness guarantee for kill switches and show how clients behave when they cannot fetch a new version.

sections.title: Requirements, APIs, and scale
sections.body: Confirm flag types (boolean, string, numeric), rule operators, user and device attributes, environment separation, SDK languages, server-side evaluation, audit and rollback needs, and target propagation time for emergency disables. At 2M evaluations/s, a central request per evaluation is an avoidable bottleneck; SDKs can perform local evaluation from cached rules in under 5 ms. The control plane handles far fewer writes, so size its database and distribution pipeline separately. A server-side POST /v1/evaluate endpoint remains available for clients that cannot safely evaluate locally. Admin APIs create and version flags and rules; GET /v1/config/{environment} returns a signed snapshot and version.

sections.title: Data model and high-level design
sections.body: Store Flag(tenant_id, environment_id, key, type, default_value, enabled, version), ordered Rule(flag_key, priority, predicate, variant), Segment(tenant_id, key, version, membership_source), and append-only AuditEvent(actor, change, timestamp). The admin API validates permissions and rule syntax, then writes configuration plus an outbox event in one relational transaction. A compiler produces a normalized, signed snapshot with a monotonically increasing environment version. A durable change stream feeds regional distribution services; edge endpoints expose the newest snapshot through long polling or server-sent events, with periodic full snapshot fetches as repair. SDKs verify signatures, atomically swap snapshots, and evaluate deterministically in memory. Evaluation telemetry is buffered and sampled asynchronously.

sections.title: Evaluation, rollout, and propagation
sections.body: Evaluate rules in explicit priority order, then fall back to the flag default. For percentage rollouts, hash a stable tuple such as tenant, flag key, and user key into a fixed bucket range; this prevents a user from randomly changing variants between requests. Validate percentage boundaries and rule syntax before publication. Every update increments a version. SDKs report their applied version and heartbeat; the console shows lagging regions and clients. For kill switches, prioritize the delta stream, use short polling intervals for active SDKs, and provide push notification where available. Mobile SDKs cannot promise immediate receipt while suspended, so state that the latest known configuration is used until reconnect.

sections.title: Reliability, security, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Keep the last valid snapshot in durable local storage and continue evaluating it during a control-plane outage; apply a configured maximum staleness policy and expose stale state to the host application. If a signature fails or a snapshot is malformed, reject it and retain the prior version. Enforce tenant-scoped authorization on writes, encrypt secrets, and avoid placing sensitive targeting attributes in telemetry. Use idempotent versioned updates, audit all edits, and support rollback by publishing a prior logical configuration as a new version. Local evaluation gives low latency and avoids a central hot path, at the cost of delayed revocation and rules being distributed to clients. Server-side evaluation protects rule confidentiality but adds network latency and service load; support both with an explicit policy.

durable-message-broker.intro: Use replicated, append-only partition logs as the durable source of truth. Separate a small strongly consistent metadata plane from the high-throughput broker data plane, and make offsets, acknowledgement rules, and failure recovery explicit.

sections.title: Requirements and capacity
sections.body: Start with durable append, replay by offset, independent consumer groups, and ordering only within a partition. Exclude global ordering and cross-partition transactions initially. At 200,000 events/s × 1 KB, average raw ingress is about 200 MB/s; seven days retains approximately 121 TB in decimal units. Three replicas require about 363 TB before indexes and overhead, with compression potentially reducing payload bytes. Peak ingress is about 1 GB/s, while replication and multiple consumer groups multiply network traffic. Benchmark sustainable per-partition throughput, then choose enough partitions and brokers to meet both peak throughput and storage requirements with failure and rebalancing headroom.

sections.title: Interfaces, records, and architecture
sections.body: Provide CreateTopic(name, partitions, retention), Produce(topic, key, producer_id, sequence, payload), Fetch(topic, partition, offset, max_bytes), and CommitOffset(group, partition, next_offset). A record contains offset, key, timestamp, checksum, producer identity/sequence, and payload. A consensus-backed metadata service stores topic definitions, leader epochs, replica membership, and group assignments. Producers cache metadata and hash keys to partitions; each partition leader appends sequential log segments and replicates them to followers across three failure domains. Consumers fetch batches by offset from partition leaders. A group coordinator leases partitions so one current group member owns each partition, while separate groups maintain independent offsets. Segments and sparse indexes support sequential reads and bounded seeks.

sections.title: Durable writes and leader recovery
sections.body: Acknowledge a record only after it is durably persisted to a majority of the three assigned replicas; make disk flush policy explicit and batch flushes to control latency. Use a consensus replication protocol per partition, or equivalent ordered-log rules, to define which prefix is committed and restrict leader election to replicas that preserve that committed prefix. Epochs fence former leaders and stale producers. On failure, elect a valid leader through the metadata/consensus plane, reconcile uncommitted tails, and retry pending writes. A lost acknowledgement creates an ambiguous outcome, so producers retry with the same producer identity and sequence; replicated deduplication state suppresses retries within the supported producer session/window. If a majority is unavailable, reject or pause writes rather than silently weaken the durability contract.

sections.title: Consumer progress, retries, and replay
sections.body: A consumer fetches from its committed next offset, processes events, then commits the next offset after successful handling. A crash after a side effect but before offset commit causes redelivery, so consumers deduplicate by stable event ID or store the business update and processed event marker in one database transaction. Offset commits alone do not make an external effect exactly once. Group membership changes create a new assignment generation; fence stale commits and revoke old ownership. New owners resume from the last committed offset. For poison events, use bounded retries and an explicit dead-letter policy; skipping an event relaxes strict processing order and must be a deliberate product choice. Retention is a time/size policy, not an infinite guarantee: alert on lag nearing expiry and return an explicit offset-out-of-range error when replay data has expired.

sections.title: Scaling, isolation, and operational tradeoffs
sections.body: Apply tenant byte-rate and storage quotas, bounded producer queues, broker disk watermarks, and retriable overload responses. Batch and compress records to improve throughput at the cost of additional latency. Hot keys still overload a single partition; split the key space only when the application accepts the changed ordering boundary. Increasing partition count can move a key between partitions, so use an explicit migration barrier or stable partition mapping when ordering must survive expansion. Rebalance replicas with bandwidth caps and preserve replication headroom. Authenticate clients, authorize topic/group access, encrypt traffic, and monitor publish latency, quorum health, disk saturation, replication lag, consumer lag, and retention headroom. Per-partition ordering scales well; global ordering collapses writes into a coordination bottleneck. A broker can guarantee durable logs and defined delivery semantics, while application side effects still require their own correctness design.

distributed-tracing.intro: Separate collecting spans from selecting and querying traces. Trace IDs connect causal spans across services, while bounded tail sampling retains useful requests without pretending that every distributed trace will be complete.

sections.title: Requirements and capacity
sections.body: Support trace-by-ID retrieval and bounded search by service, error status, duration, and time. Target visibility within 30 seconds after collector acceptance, and seven-day retention for sampled traces. Define a maximum assembly window and how late spans are displayed. Peak ingress is 1 GB/s at 2M spans/s and 500 bytes/span. If that peak were sustained, raw storage would be 604.8 TB for seven days. A 5% byte retention assumption gives roughly 30.2 TB of payload before replicas and indexes; actual cost depends on average traffic, compression, and the proportion of errors and slow traces. Measure span size and trace length distributions to size the stream, collector memory, and tail sampling window.

sections.title: APIs and data model
sections.body: SDKs export batches with stable (trace_id, span_id), parent_span_id, service, start timestamp, duration, status, and bounded attributes. Derive tenant identity from authenticated credentials. ExportSpans returns an explicit acceptance or retriable overload result. GET /v1/traces/{id} reads a trace manifest and payload chunks; search accepts bounded time ranges, allowlisted service/status filters, minimum duration, and cursor pagination. Partition storage and all lookup keys by tenant. Store a trace summary with root duration when known, participating services, error flags, completeness status, chunk references, and sampling reason. Persist spans independently so a missing parent does not discard useful evidence.

sections.title: High-level ingestion and query design
sections.body: SDKs create trace/span IDs and propagate context through outgoing requests. A local collector batches, compresses, and retries with bounded buffers. An authenticated ingest tier validates schema, enforces quotas, and acknowledges only after the batch reaches the chosen durability boundary in a replicated stream. Partition by a hash of tenant and trace ID to place a trace on one assembly owner. Stateful workers collect spans, evaluate tail sampling rules, and write retained chunks plus a versioned manifest to object storage. A separate idempotent indexer reads finalized summaries into a time-partitioned search store. Trace lookup reads the manifest directly; search returns IDs and summaries, followed by payload retrieval on demand. Track stream lag and indexing lag against the visibility target.

sections.title: Tail sampling, lateness, and recovery
sections.body: Within a bounded window, retain error traces and slow traces, then deterministically sample ordinary traces by trace ID. Tail sampling must receive spans before deciding, so store assembly state in a bounded keyed store with a checkpoint/changelog that can recover after worker failure. Keep sampling decisions for a defined late-arrival interval. Append late spans to retained traces and update manifests and searchable summaries. If a late error arrives for a previously dropped trace, retain that late evidence as a partial trace; earlier discarded spans cannot be reconstructed without a raw retention buffer. Use a short raw stream retention window for optional reassembly, with explicit storage cost. Deduplicate retries by tenant/trace/span ID and use idempotent chunk/index writes. A finite waiting window bounds latency and memory but cannot guarantee complete traces.

sections.title: Isolation, failure behavior, and tradeoffs
sections.body: SDK buffers must have hard byte limits and drop policies, exporting drop counters without blocking application requests. Collectors can spool to disk within quota; once full, reject new batches or shed lower-priority telemetry visibly. Head sampling is cheaper but can discard errors before their outcome is known; tail sampling captures outcomes at higher buffering and routing cost. Never claim all production errors are retained when SDKs can drop spans or a tenant exceeds quota: the target applies to eligible spans received by collectors within the stated policy. Sanitize sensitive attributes, cap attribute sizes, and index only approved fields to prevent cardinality explosions. Use parent IDs for causality and per-span durations for timing; cross-host clock skew makes exact global timestamp order unreliable. Monitor accepted/dropped spans, partial traces, sampling reasons, memory pressure, queue age, query latency, tenant usage, and storage expiry. Keep metrics and logging operationally independent enough to diagnose a tracing outage.

game-leaderboard.intro: Treat accepted score events as durable facts and the ranking index as a recoverable view. Define a total order and snapshot version so that “exact rank” has a precise meaning even while scores are changing.

sections.title: Requirements and sizing
sections.body: Support trusted score submissions, top 100, exact personal rank, and nearby players, ordered by descending integer score then ascending player ID. Clarify whether score decreases are legal; support them with serialized per-player updates. Normal freshness is at most two seconds after acceptance, while responses expose the applied snapshot version. Fifty million minimal 64-byte records occupy about 3.2 GB raw, but a practical ranked index and replication consume much more. Peak accepted events at 100K/s and 200 bytes/event are roughly 20 MB/s before replication. Benchmark update and rank operations to decide whether a single ordered index meets the target; capacity alone does not establish throughput.

sections.title: Interfaces and durable acceptance
sections.body: SubmitScore includes season, player, globally unique event_id and delta; derive server authority from credentials and reject untrusted clients. In a transactional durable store, a unique event_id prevents double application and a per-player version serializes concurrent score changes. Commit the new player score, accepted event, and outbox record atomically, then return an acceptance version. The API offers top, rank, and neighbors queries keyed by season. Store Season(state, cutoff, final_snapshot), PlayerScore(season, player, score, version), AcceptedScoreEvent(event_id, payload_hash, player_version), and ordered ranking entries keyed by (negative_score, player_id). Reusing an event ID with a different payload is rejected.

sections.title: Baseline architecture and recovery
sections.body: Authenticated API → durable score database and outbox → ordered event stream → ranked-view worker → replicated ordered index → query API and short-lived top-100 cache. Use an order-statistic tree, or a sorted structure with rank operations, so insert/remove/rank cost O(log N). A single view owner applies a player’s versioned old-to-new score change atomically, ignores already-applied versions, and buffers or repairs version gaps from authoritative state. Snapshot the index with its stream checkpoint and replay after failure. A query reads one committed index version; rank is one plus the number of entries preceding the player. Nearby queries seek around the player’s total-order key. Return both view version and data age, and allow callers to wait for an acceptance version when they require read-after-write behavior.

sections.title: Scaling exact ranks across score ranges
sections.body: If the baseline cannot sustain measured load, partition the total order into contiguous score/key ranges with an ordered index and count per range. Exact global rank equals counts of preceding ranges plus local rank, but all terms must come from the same snapshot. Use a transactional, versioned index store: moving a player across ranges removes the old key, adds the new key, and updates range counts in one distributed transaction. MVCC snapshot reads give a consistent player key, preceding counts, and local rank at one timestamp; an independently updated counter cache cannot provide this guarantee. Split hot ranges using the full (score, player_id) key so a popular tied score can span shards. Top K merges the earliest ordered ranges at the same snapshot. Distributed transactions and range-count contention are real costs; benchmark them and offer a bounded-staleness snapshot rather than labeling mixed-time reads exact.

sections.title: Season closure, reliability, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Close a season by atomically changing its state to closing and recording an admission cutoff; reject later submissions. Drain every accepted outbox event through that cutoff, wait for the view checkpoints to catch up, and write a versioned immutable final snapshot before marking the season closed. Reconcile index entries and counts against authoritative scores periodically; use rate limits, payload validation, audit trails and anti-cheat checks at trusted ingestion. Monitor acceptance latency, view lag, version gaps, cross-range transaction aborts, count contention and query age. Read replicas and caches can serve a published snapshot but may be stale. A single ordered owner is simpler and gives atomic rank updates; sharding improves capacity while making exact global ranks and score moves more expensive. The durable store and replay log preserve accepted updates even if a ranking cache is lost.

distributed-lock-service.intro: Use consensus to serialize lease grants and monotonically increasing fencing tokens to reject obsolete owners at the protected resource. Lease expiry enables progress, while downstream validation provides the safety that a paused client cannot provide for itself.

sections.title: Requirements and capacity
sections.body: Agree on resource-level exclusive grants, bounded lease TTLs, owner identity, waiting policy, retry semantics, and the downstream fencing contract. One million 200-byte active records require roughly 200 MB raw before replicas, history and deduplication. With 30-second TTLs and renewal every 10 seconds, a million continuously held leases generate about 100K renewals/s before acquisition and release traffic. The initial 100K/s total budget therefore has no spare capacity: choose a smaller simultaneously renewing population, longer TTLs, or a higher measured capacity. Size shard count from consensus-write benchmarks and hot-resource contention, not memory size alone.

sections.title: API, data model, and routing
sections.body: Acquire(resource, owner, request_id, ttl) returns a unique lease_id, per-resource generation and TTL after durable commit, or a busy response. Renew requires lease_id and generation and must fail for obsolete or already expired ownership. Release conditionally removes only that exact active lease; a delayed release cannot delete a successor. Persist request_id with a request hash and original outcome for bounded retry deduplication. Retrying an old acquire must never create a second lease silently; expose whether the original grant is still active. Each record includes resource, lease identity, owner, generation, TTL/expiry state and revision. Hash resource names to consensus groups; a resource has exactly one authoritative group during routing changes.

sections.title: Consensus, expiration, and failover
sections.body: Route mutations to a shard leader replicated across three failure domains. Acquire is a committed conditional transition from free to held that increments the durable per-resource generation; retain generation metadata after release so tokens never reset for a reused resource name. Renew and release are also ordered consensus commands. Expiration is a committed transition conditional on the current lease identity and renewal revision, so a queued expiration cannot cancel a renewal already ordered before it. Use monotonic local timers rather than trusting client clocks. On leader change, recover committed state and conservatively wait at least the maximum supported lease TTL before expiring recovered leases if remaining time cannot be established safely; this delays availability but avoids premature regranting under ambiguous elapsed time. Clients treat renewal timeout as loss of authority and stop protected work. A majority is required for grants; a minority partition cannot issue new ownership.

sections.title: Fencing paused clients at the resource
sections.body: A client may pause past expiry and later resume while a new owner is working. Include the monotonically increasing generation on every protected write. The downstream store atomically compares the token against its per-resource highest accepted token in the same transaction as the mutation, rejecting smaller tokens. A successor must install its token through a fencing barrier before treating itself as admitted to the protected resource; after that barrier all older writes are rejected. Writes by an old client before that barrier may still have committed, so describe this guarantee precisely. Multiple writes from the same generation are allowed only under the application’s owner and sequencing policy; use idempotency keys for retried side effects. For an external API that cannot enforce fencing or equivalent conditional updates, this service can provide advisory coordination but cannot promise exclusion of stale effects.

sections.title: Waiting, recovery, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Use revision-based watches: first read the busy lease with a revision, then watch from that revision so a release between read and subscription is not lost. If history is compacted, reread and restart. Add bounded wait queues, jittered retry, tenant quotas and cancellation so one hot lock does not exhaust a shard. Fairness requires a durable ordered waiter policy and comes with extra state; a simple retry API is not strictly FIFO. Shard migration needs a fenced routing epoch and one authoritative grant path so old and new groups cannot both grant. Monitor grant latency, renewal failures, expired leases, consensus quorum health, hot keys, watch fanout, fencing rejections and deduplication retention. Short TTLs recover abandoned work sooner but increase renewal load and sensitivity to pauses; longer TTLs reduce traffic but delay takeover. Multi-resource atomic locking and cross-region synchronous availability require additional coordination beyond the initial scope.

package-registry.intro: Keep immutable, digest-addressed artifact bytes separate from transactional package metadata. Publish a version only after its artifact is verified and durable, and make provenance, namespace ownership, and revocation semantics explicit.

sections.title: Requirements and capacity
sections.body: Support scoped public/private namespaces, immutable package versions, dependency manifests, mutable distribution tags, authenticated publication and quarantine. A version tuple cannot be overwritten even after quarantine; retain a tombstone if bytes are later deleted. Ten million versions at 5 MB average require about 50 TB raw storage, with another 5 TB/day at one million publishes/day before replication. Peak downloads need roughly 100 GB/s of artifact egress, so cache immutable bytes at a CDN and serve small metadata separately. Estimate metadata object sizes, cache hit rate, scanning throughput and retention to size databases and workers. State a 30-second normal propagation target and define stronger publish confirmation separately.

sections.title: APIs and data model
sections.body: POST /upload-sessions creates a scoped staging upload; POST /packages/{name}/versions finalizes an artifact using an idempotency key, version, manifest and expected digest. GET package metadata returns available versions, manifests and tag revision with an ETag; GET a version returns its immutable digest and provenance. Conditional tag updates require a matching prior revision. Download authorization resolves a package/version to the verified blob rather than granting arbitrary digest access. Store Namespace and membership, Package, Version(namespace,name,version,digest,manifest,state), Blob(digest,size,storage_state), Tag(package,name,target,revision), PublishRequest and append-only AuditEvent. Enforce a unique constraint on namespace/name/version and compare payload hashes when idempotency keys repeat.

sections.title: Publication and installation architecture
sections.body: Maintainer → authenticated API → upload session → staging object store → validation/scanning workers → immutable artifact store → transactional metadata service and outbox → cache invalidation/index workers. Verify the uploaded digest and archive size, validate the manifest, and complete the required durable object replication before marking the blob ready. A metadata transaction can then publish the version and its outbox event; metadata must never reference an unfinished staging upload. If the transaction fails, retain the orphan for delayed cleanup. Clients fetch metadata with conditional requests, resolve dependencies according to one supported versioning scheme, and write exact versions plus integrity digests into lockfiles. Installs using lockfiles fetch immutable artifacts via CDN and verify downloaded bytes against the recorded digest. The initial design keeps dependency solving on clients; a server resolver would additionally need explicit snapshot/version semantics.

sections.title: Integrity, tenancy, and compromised releases
sections.body: Use scoped publisher credentials, namespace ownership checks, short-lived upload tokens, audit logs and optional signed provenance tied to a build identity. Keep private package metadata out of shared public caches. For private downloads, authorize before serving cached bytes, include access scope in the cache policy, and bound token lifetime; digest equality is not authorization. Enforce explicit registry/namespace mappings to reduce dependency confusion rather than automatically preferring a public package with the same name. Quarantine changes mutable metadata, invalidates caches, blocks new authorized downloads and records a durable tombstone. Short-lived download tokens and edge revocation checks bound propagation, but bytes already downloaded or installed cannot be recalled. A CDN purge alone is not a universal immediate-revocation guarantee; publish a maximum revocation window and require online policy checks where stricter behavior is needed.

sections.title: Failure recovery and tradeoffs
sections.body: Concurrent publishes serialize on the immutable version key. Retried finalize calls return the original result; an object-store success followed by a database failure is repaired through idempotent retry or delayed orphan collection. Store tag updates with compare-and-set revision checks so competing releases cannot silently overwrite each other. Outbox consumers are idempotent and can replay invalidations and search indexing. Give immutable blobs long cache lifetimes; mutable metadata uses short TTLs and validators, with quarantine checks outside an indefinitely cached artifact URL. Garbage collection must prove no published references exist and use a grace period longer than upload/retry windows, protected by a reference/GC state protocol against concurrent publication. Monitor missing-blob errors, publish lag, scan backlog, origin bandwidth, metadata cache age, authorization failures and quarantine propagation. Replicated read metadata improves availability but can be briefly stale; the authoritative publish endpoint returns the committed version while global caches converge.

stack.tradeoff: Object durability and metadata commit are separate. Keep a grace period for orphan cleanup.

secrets-manager.intro: Separate authorization, encrypted version storage, and rotation orchestration. Use short-lived workload identity, envelope encryption, and explicit policy freshness so the service’s access guarantees remain clear during caching and regional failures.

sections.title: Requirements and capacity
sections.body: Support immutable versions, controlled current-version aliases, tenant-scoped access, rotation, audit and recoverable deletion. Clarify whether dynamic credentials are required in addition to stored static secrets. Ten million 2 KB versions are about 20 GB of plaintext-equivalent payload; metadata, wrapped keys, replicas and audit history may dominate storage. Peak read payload is about 200 MB/s before protocol overhead. At 500 bytes/event and 100K reads/s sustained, audit ingress is 50 MB/s or 4.32 TB/day. Benchmark identity verification, policy evaluation, key-service calls and network latency against the 100 ms regional target. Promise the 60-second revocation bound for online authorization checks, while separately describing existing client copies and downstream credential validity.

sections.title: API and data model
sections.body: Expose CreateVersion with a request ID, ReadSecret with an explicit version or alias, conditional alias updates, Rotate and policy administration. Derive tenant and workload identity from verified short-lived credentials, never a caller-supplied tenant header alone. Store Secret(tenant,id,state), Version(secret,version,ciphertext,wrapped_data_key,key_id,encryption_context), Alias(secret,name,target,revision), Policy(scope,rules,revision), RotationJob(id,state,external_reference) and append-only AuditEvent(request,principal,secret,version,decision,policy_revision). A unique request ID with payload comparison makes version creation idempotent. Secret bodies are omitted from application logs, traces and audit events.

sections.title: Read/write architecture and encryption
sections.body: For each new version, generate a fresh data encryption key through a managed key service, encrypt with an authenticated cipher using tenant/secret/version as associated context, and persist the ciphertext plus wrapped key after a durable transaction. The key service retains the wrapping key under its access controls. Regional read services authenticate workload identity, evaluate the current permitted policy, select a version and fetch its ciphertext. Only an authorized service path unwraps the data key and decrypts; TLS protects the response. Cache ciphertext freely within tenant boundaries, while any plaintext/data-key cache is bounded, isolated and reauthorized on every read. Commit write metadata and an outbox event atomically for replication and invalidation. Authoritative write confirmation is distinct from asynchronous cross-region visibility.

sections.title: Policy freshness, audits, and outages
sections.body: Publish policy changes with monotonically increasing revisions and push invalidations to regions. A region may authorize from a cached policy only while its last successful authoritative refresh is younger than the 60-second revocation limit, with a conservative allowance for processing delay; once stale, fail closed until refreshed. This trades availability for the stated online-read bound during partitions. Do not permit a long-lived bearer token to bypass the policy check. Record an access-decision event durably before returning secret bytes when audit durability is mandatory; if the audit pipeline cannot accept it, reject the read rather than silently lose the audit. The event proves an authorized disclosure attempt, not that a remote client received the response. A key-service outage can use only explicitly approved short-lived key caches; otherwise decryption fails closed. Monitor authorization age, denied reads, decrypt errors, audit lag and cross-tenant access anomalies.

sections.title: Rotation, revocation, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Run rotation as a durable state machine: generate a new external credential, store a pending encrypted version, verify it against the target system, conditionally switch the current alias, wait a defined client migration interval, and revoke the old external credential. Serialize rotations per secret and use idempotent external operation IDs or reconciliation queries so retries do not create uncontrolled credentials. Recover by observing which steps succeeded; no atomic transaction spans an external database and the secrets metadata store. When the target supports two active credentials, overlap enables safe rollout; otherwise rotation may require a coordinated maintenance window. Revoking registry read permission cannot remove cached client bytes or disable a static password at its target. Revoke the external credential or use short-lived dynamic credentials to bound that exposure, accounting for target-side revocation semantics. Encrypt backups, restrict and audit break-glass access, test restore procedures and retain deletion tombstones. Faster policy revocation and less plaintext caching increase dependence on online services; document that tradeoff rather than promising both indefinite offline access and immediate revocation.

document-search-engine.intro: Use an inverted index as a recoverable projection of authoritative versioned documents. Separate candidate retrieval and ranking from final permission checks so an index-refresh delay never becomes permission to disclose document content.

sections.title: Requirements and capacity
sections.body: Support term and phrase queries, explicit filters, ranked pages, versioned updates and deletion, with normal searchable freshness within 30 seconds. Define whether the 300 ms p95 target applies only when every shard responds or permits marked partial results. One billion documents at 5 KB require roughly 5 TB raw text; postings, stored positions, replicas, tombstones and compaction headroom add workload-dependent overhead. Peak 50K updates/s is about 250 MB/s before replication and analysis. Use representative document/query distributions to measure index bytes per document and query CPU rather than inventing a fixed expansion ratio. Provision replicas for 20K QPS and enough ingestion capacity to keep freshness bounded during segment merges.

sections.title: APIs and authoritative data
sections.body: PUT /documents/{id} carries tenant-scoped identity, content, metadata and a monotonically increasing document version; use conditional updates and deduplicate retry keys. DELETE creates a versioned tombstone. POST /search accepts query text, allowlisted filters, page size and an opaque cursor. Store authoritative Document(tenant,id,version,content_ref,metadata,state), Policy/ACL revision and an outbox event in the same transaction. Inverted postings map each analyzed term to document IDs, term frequencies and positions; positions enable phrase matching. Keep document length and ranking features alongside searchable fields. Acknowledged source writes are durable independently of when they become searchable.

sections.title: Indexing pipeline and high-level architecture
sections.body: Authenticated ingest API → replicated document store and outbox → durable change stream → analyzer workers → document-partitioned index shards with replicas. Route all updates for one document to the same partition and apply only newer document versions; delayed older events cannot resurrect a deleted document. Normalize text consistently at indexing and query time, tokenize by language, and persist term positions. Workers buffer updates then publish immutable segments and an atomic segment manifest; refresh makes new segments visible within the target. Background merges compact segments and tombstones while respecting active reader snapshots. Checkpoint the stream only after a recoverable index commit. Restore a shard from snapshots and replay its stream, or rebuild from the authoritative source.

sections.title: Query execution, ranking, and pagination
sections.body: A coordinator resolves the tenant’s shard set and sends an analyzed query to one healthy replica per shard. Each shard intersects or unions postings according to the query, tests phrase positions and metadata filters, scores matching documents with a defined relevance function, and returns its top candidates. Merge by score with a stable document-ID tie-break. If scores must be comparable across shards, use shared ranking statistics from a published statistics snapshot; independent shard-local statistics can distort global ordering. Enforce query limits and deadlines. On timeout, either fail the query or return visibly partial results according to the agreed contract. Use a point-in-time index snapshot with search-after cursors for stable deep pagination, expiring snapshots to bound retained segments. A page assembled across different refresh states is not a globally transactional document snapshot.

sections.title: Permissions, deletes, and operational tradeoffs
sections.body: Treat search hits as untrusted candidates until a batch authorization service checks the current policy and current document state. Perform this check before creating snippets, fetching protected fields or revealing titles; never return stale cached snippets solely because the index says access was allowed. If authorization is unavailable, fail closed for protected results. Recheck access on document retrieval as well. Over-fetch and refill candidates within a bounded budget when authorization removes hits, while keeping exact counts, facets and timing from leaking protected document existence; suppress or permission-filter those aggregates. Delete tombstones hide documents immediately at the authoritative disclosure gate while async index cleanup and backup retention follow explicit policies. Revalidate ACLs even for stable point-in-time pagination. Isolate large tenants, cap expensive queries, and monitor refresh age, merge backlog, shard skew, candidate rejection rates, authorization latency and partial responses. More frequent refresh improves freshness but creates more segments and merge work; term sharding reduces some query fanout but complicates joins and hot-term handling, so begin with document sharding.

stack.reason: Use conditional versions and an outbox transaction for document metadata and ACL revisions, with immutable content in S3.
stack.tradeoff: Cross-region replicas can lag. Final disclosure needs an authoritative permission decision.

stack.reason: Relay outbox records into a replayable Kafka topic keyed by tenant and document ID.
stack.tradeoff: The relay can redeliver. The index projector must reject stale versions and preserve tombstones.

stack.name: Elasticsearch
stack.reason: Use language analyzers, term positions for phrases, BM25 ranking and point-in-time pagination.
stack.tradeoff: The index is eventually consistent. Check current ACLs before returning any protected text.

content-delivery-network.intro: Keep request serving local to the edge, and distribute versioned routing and invalidation state through a separate control plane. Cache correctness depends on the complete cache key, eligibility rules, and how purge generations interact with in-flight origin fetches.

sections.title: Requirements and capacity
sections.body: Start with GET/HEAD caching, public immutable assets and explicitly cacheable mutable responses. Define personalized/private behavior, TLS custom domains, purge scope, range requests and allowed stale serving. At 1M requests/s with 100 KB mean cacheable payload, peak edge egress is around 100 GB/s or 800 Gb/s before overhead. A 95% request hit ratio leaves roughly 50K cache misses/s; origin bytes are not necessarily 5% of total because object sizes and popularity differ. Size edge memory/disk tiers from measured working sets and shield caches from regional miss traffic. The 50 ms edge-processing target excludes user-to-edge network latency; state both metrics separately.

sections.title: APIs, cache records, and control plane
sections.body: Customer APIs configure verified domains, origins, TLS settings and cache policy; POST /purges accepts an exact URL or tag scope plus an idempotency key, and GET /purges/{id} exposes propagation status. Store tenant/domain routing, origin allowlist, policy revision and durable purge generations in a replicated control store with audit history. A cache key includes tenant/domain, normalized path and allowed query components plus every request attribute needed for the cached representation. Record body reference, status, selected headers, ETag, Last-Modified, expiry, Vary dimensions, policy revision and the purge generations observed when filling. Push signed/versioned configuration and purge events to regions, with snapshot resynchronization when replay history is unavailable.

sections.title: High-level request path and stampede control
sections.body: Traffic steering sends clients to a healthy nearby point of presence. The edge terminates TLS, validates host routing and any required authorization, derives the canonical key, and checks a memory/disk cache. A fresh eligible hit returns locally. A miss uses one in-flight fetch per key per cache node so followers share the result. Regional shields coalesce misses across edges before contacting the origin, reducing flash-crowd load. Apply origin concurrency budgets, deadlines and bounded queues; add TTL jitter and proactive refresh for known hot keys. For stale entries, conditional requests with validators can reuse a body after a 304 response. Respect cache-control directives; do not cache responses carrying user-specific state under a public shared key. Treat range caching as a defined whole-object or chunked policy rather than mixing incompatible byte ranges.

sections.title: Purge ordering and bounded propagation
sections.body: Assign a durable increasing purge generation per tenant/scope. Edges invalidate matching entries and remember generations long enough to reject old cached objects and delayed fills. An origin fetch captures its relevant generation before starting; before installing or serving the fetched object, compare it with the latest applied generation and discard/revalidate if a purge raced with the fill. This closes the common hole where an old in-flight response repopulates an already purged key. Track acknowledgement by active serving edge and expose pending, completed or failed states. For the 60-second serving bound, require a short renewable serving lease tied to successful control-plane synchronization; lagging or disconnected edges stop serving affected tenant traffic before the bound and require resynchronization to rejoin. Steering changes alone cannot stop existing connections, so the edge must enforce that lease locally. Define a conservative timing margin and validate clock/lease assumptions. Never mark a purge globally completed solely because it was queued.

sections.title: Security, origin failure, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Reject unverified hostnames and route origins only through customer-approved destinations, with protection against internal-address fetches and redirects that escape the allowlist. Bound headers and object sizes, normalize keys consistently, and allowlist Vary dimensions to avoid poisoning and unbounded key cardinality. For private content, authorize before cache hits and scope cache entries or bypass shared caching; a signed URL’s lifetime and revocation policy determine access bounds. During origin failure, serve stale only where policy allows and never override a purge or authorization failure with stale fallback. Fail over shields and regions with origin rate limits to avoid a recovery stampede. Monitor request and byte hit ratios, origin fanout, fill-coalescing rates, tail latency, stale age, purge lag, lease expiry and egress. Pull caching reduces storage replication but has cold misses; long TTLs improve hit rates but need reliable invalidation. A CDN purge prevents future edge disclosure under the contract but cannot erase browser caches or previously downloaded copies.

distributed-analytics-query.intro: Use a coordinator to pin input snapshots and break each SQL query into stages. Workers scan immutable files and exchange intermediate data. A durable query record and an atomic result manifest give callers a clear view of completed work.

sections.title: Requirements and sizing
sections.body: Start with read-only SQL and approximate capacity from bytes actually scanned. Pin one catalog snapshot per table at submission or planning, then document that each table is repeatable. If statements must see a common multi-table point in time, the catalog must offer a shared commit boundary. At 40 GB per eligible dashboard query and a 30-second objective, the scan alone needs about 1.3 GB/s. Two hundred equivalent scans would need around 267 GB/s aggregate before shuffle and processing. Reserve an execution budget smaller than the total latency target and confirm admission limits through load testing. Long batch jobs can trade queue time for throughput.

sections.title: API and data model
sections.body: POST /queries takes SQL, workload class, and an idempotency key and returns a query ID. GET /queries/{id} returns status, bytes scanned, and an error if the job fails. POST /queries/{id}/cancel requests cancellation. GET /queries/{id}/results takes an opaque cursor bound to the completed result manifest. Store Query(id, tenant, principal, statement hash, state, deadline, snapshots), StageAttempt(query, stage, partition, generation, output reference), and ResultManifest(page references, schema, expiry). Authorize catalog access when planning, apply row and column policies at execution, and verify current access before returning saved results. Treat generated SQL and query IDs as inputs requiring validation and authorization.

sections.title: Plan and execute a query
sections.body: The query API authenticates and durably records a request. An admission controller meters each tenant and separates dashboard and batch queues. The coordinator resolves table snapshot manifests and builds a plan. Push filters and column selection into workers that read file splits from object storage. In a query that groups sales by region, workers can compute local totals, shuffle partial totals to workers responsible for each region, and combine them. Broadcast only a join input that safely fits in worker memory. Partition both large inputs by join key for a larger join. Store final pages in object storage and publish a manifest atomically when all results are ready.

sections.title: Recover from failures
sections.body: Give each task attempt its own output location. The coordinator selects one accepted attempt per logical partition and records that choice before downstream stages consume its output. After a worker fails, reschedule missing tasks against the same snapshot. Readers use the accepted manifest and cannot see a retry’s partial output. For coordinator loss, recover recorded decisions under a fenced coordinator lease. An older coordinator cannot publish after ownership changes. If the plan state is insufficient for recovery, restart the query from its pinned inputs within its retry and deadline budget, or mark it failed. Use compare-and-set terminal states so cancel and publish have a clear winner. Reclaim abandoned attempt files after a grace period.

sections.title: Skew, isolation, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Use separate execution pools or reserved capacity for dashboard traffic and enforce per-tenant memory, scan bytes, and concurrency ceilings. Prune partitions and project only needed columns. Track the largest task versus the median to detect skew. For grouped sums, split an oversized key across workers for partial aggregation, then combine those partials under the original key. Use spill or a durable shuffle for long jobs where recomputing intermediate work is expensive. In-memory exchange saves writes on small queries but can require stage recomputation after a failure. Monitor queue time separately from execution time, and report bytes scanned, shuffle bytes, spill, retries, and tenant saturation.

experiment-analysis-platform.intro: Keep a durable record of assignments and outcomes, then compute each metric from the eligible cohort and a versioned analysis plan. Use streaming for monitoring and a reproducible batch pass for the final result.

sections.title: Requirements and capacity
sections.body: Start with user-level experiments and a binary conversion outcome per enrolled user. Set eligibility before randomization, freeze the randomization unit and allocation within a version, and agree on the enrollment period, outcome window, and lateness allowance. If assignments occur only when users reach a feature, treat that pre-variant event as the eligibility boundary. Keep observed exposures as diagnostics. Average ingest is 20,000 × 350 bytes, about 7 MB/s. At that steady rate, 30 days require about 18.1 TB of raw storage. Three copies would be roughly 54.4 TB before compression. Peak ingest of 35 MB/s informs queue partitions and worker capacity. Keep the raw retention period longer than the longest supported experiment, outcome window, and lateness combined, or snapshot immutable report inputs before they expire.

sections.title: Interfaces and records
sections.body: POST /experiments creates an immutable experiment version with allocation, eligible population, primary metric, and analysis window. POST /events accepts batches with stable event IDs, authenticated source, user ID, event time, and event type. GET /experiments/{id}/results returns a report revision, counts by arm, data completeness, rates, and uncertainty. Store Assignment(experiment version, user, arm, enrolled_at), Exposure(experiment version, user, arm, shown_at), Outcome(event_id, user, event_time, type), and Report(experiment version, metric definition version, input snapshot IDs, cutoff, status). Keep identifiers pseudonymous and apply tenant permissions, retention, and deletion rules to raw events and derived views.

sections.title: Ingest and attribute
sections.body: A stable hash of experiment ID, version, and user ID assigns a variant under the frozen allocation. Write the enrollment record through a reliable event path before applying the variant and require that retries reuse the same assignment key. Ingest accepts events once durably buffered, then stores raw events in object storage for replay. Partition the join by experiment version and user. Keep one enrollment per user, deduplicate event IDs, and wait for late assignments or outcomes within a known event-time allowance. Join outcomes inside each user’s observation window. For conversion, reduce each user to a yes/no result. Count all enrolled users in the denominator so deciding whether someone was exposed after assignment cannot selectively filter out a treatment group.

sections.title: Check and publish
sections.body: Use streaming materialized views for provisional counts and show their data freshness and completeness. Compare observed assignment proportions with expected allocation using a sample ratio mismatch check. Treat a failing check as a data quality signal and withhold a recommendation while checking eligibility, enrollment delivery, and event loss by arm. Separately compare exposure and outcome delivery rates, since a matching assignment ratio cannot prove later telemetry is healthy. At the preset cutoff, recompute from deduplicated raw snapshots after waiting for the outcome and lateness windows. Publish an immutable report revision with rates, treatment-control difference, and a confidence interval. Apply inference at the randomization unit. If a correction is needed later, publish a new revision with the reason, preserving the old one.

sections.title: Failures and tradeoffs
sections.body: Checkpoint stream progress and let replay rebuild provisional views after worker loss. Key aggregates and report writes by version so retries replace or reconcile the same logical work. Quarantine malformed records and alert when lag or missing data exceeds budget. A 15-minute view helps spot instrumentation bugs and guardrail regressions. Use the planned analysis cutoff for ordinary fixed-horizon inference, or use a method designed for repeated looks if early decisions are required. Separate exploratory segments and additional metrics from the predeclared primary result. Batch reconciliation costs extra compute but makes reports reproducible. Handling all enrolled users can dilute effects when few see the change, but filtering by observed exposure after randomization can bias the comparison.

nearby-place-search.intro: Use a searchable view of versioned place listings. Route each query to the geographic shards that could hold a match, then filter candidates by actual distance before ranking them.

sections.title: Requirements and scale
sections.body: Support text, category, straight-line radius, and an optional open-now filter. Use a conservative rectangle or other complete region cover for routing, then check a documented earth-distance model. Keep travel-time routing outside this version. At 100 million listings and about 1 KB of indexed fields each, the raw documents contribute about 100 GB before spatial indexes, text postings, and replicas. Four shard queries per search on average produces 200,000 shard requests/s at peak. Measure the distribution of fan-out and candidate counts, especially downtown, since the average does not size the busiest partition.

sections.title: API and records
sections.body: GET /places/search accepts latitude, longitude, radiusMeters, optional query, category and openNow, and an opaque cursor. Return listing IDs, summaries, distance and an explicit partial-results flag if coverage is incomplete. GET /places/{id} reads the current source record. PUT /places/{id} with an expected version lets authorized owners update listings, including a coordinate move or closure. Store id, coordinates, names and categories, timezone, weekly hours and exceptions, status, and version. Evaluate open-now at a captured query timestamp using the listing timezone, including holiday and overnight rules.

sections.title: Writes and index consistency
sections.body: Store the listing and an outbox record in the same transaction. Publish the change to an indexing queue. The projector applies updates and tombstones with a version fence so delayed events cannot resurrect a closed or outdated listing. If coordinates move across shards, write the new version and a tombstone to the old shard, then reconcile until both are visible. During the transition, deduplicate returned IDs and validate the displayed candidate version against authoritative metadata before returning changes that affect eligibility. Measure source-to-index lag and replay the outbox after failure. Search can still temporarily omit a moved listing until the new projection appears.

sections.title: Read, rank, and page
sections.body: Cover the requested circle with a conservative set of routing cells or intersecting shard regions. Handle longitude wraparound when a cover crosses the antimeridian and avoid dropping edge cells based on their centers. Each shard combines a spatial index and text postings to get candidates, then applies exact distance, availability, and category checks. Rank with a common scoring function that combines text fit, distance and a quality signal. The coordinator merges shard top lists, applies deterministic ID tie-breaks, and refills when deduplication or validation drops candidates. When strict paging is required, use a short-lived per-shard snapshot and bind the cursor to it, with the query radius, score definition, and evaluation timestamp.

sections.title: Load, failure, and tradeoffs
sections.body: Replicate popular areas, split dense shards, set query deadlines, and enforce radius and page limits. A failed required shard can be retried on a replica. If the time budget expires, either fail the request or clearly label partial coverage and avoid offering a normal continuation cursor. A coarse cell cover keeps routing simple but creates more false candidates. Finer cells can increase routing fan-out and metadata. A cache keyed only by a rough location is unsafe for final results near a radius edge. Cache a wider pool of candidates when useful and recheck exact distance and time-sensitive eligibility. Track p95 by region, candidate volume, fan-out, stale-version drops, index lag, and partial responses.
