stack.name: Go + H3
stack.role: Search API, routing, and result merge.
stack.reason: Use a Go coordinator to cover the search circle with intersecting H3 cells, select all relevant regions, and merge results.
stack.tradeoff: A cover based on cell centers can miss edge matches. Use a conservative cover and independent distance verification.

stack.name: MySQL (InnoDB)
stack.reason: Commit a listing revision and its index event together. Use expected versions to reject stale edits.
stack.tradeoff: Authoritative writes are visible before the search projection catches up. Store and serve version information.

stack.name: Debezium + Apache Kafka
stack.reason: Read MySQL outbox changes from the binlog and publish by listing ID for a replayable indexing path.
stack.tradeoff: Retries can redeliver records. Use listing versions to apply old-shard tombstones and repeat updates safely.

stack.name: Elasticsearch
stack.reason: Index text, categories, and geo_point coordinates. Apply a geo_distance filter before ranking candidates.
stack.tradeoff: Search refresh and shard moves create a window of staleness. Deduplicate and check versions before returning results.

systems.title: Design a rate limiter
systems.scenario: Design a rate limiter for a public API handling 1M requests per second across multiple regions.
guide: Clarify whether limits are per user, key, or endpoint and what consistency is required.
Compare token bucket, leaky bucket, and sliding window; explain the tradeoffs.
Choose an enforcement point and discuss distributed counters, hot keys, regional behavior, and cache.
Cover failure policy, abuse resistance, observability, and how you would test limits at scale.

systems.title: Design a URL shortener
systems.scenario: Design a URL shortener that supports 100M new links each month and fast global redirects.
guide: Estimate read/write volume and define expiry, custom aliases, and redirect requirements.
Choose an ID generation strategy and data model; discuss collision handling.
Cover cache, database partitioning, global reads, and consistency.
Add abuse controls, analytics, and operational metrics.

systems.title: Design a notification service
systems.scenario: Design a service that delivers email, push, and SMS notifications to 50M users.
guide: Clarify delivery guarantees, priority, preferences, and per-channel constraints.
Design queues and workers with deduplication, retries, and backoff.
Discuss provider failures, rate limits, ordering, and dead-letter handling.
Define delivery observability, privacy controls, and capacity planning.

systems.title: Design a news feed
systems.scenario: Design a personalized home feed for 100M users with low-latency reads.
guide: Compare fan-out on write and fan-out on read, including celebrity accounts.
Describe ranking inputs, pagination, and feed freshness.
Design cache keys and invalidation while managing hot users.
Discuss storage growth, backfills, and feed quality metrics.

systems.title: Design a file storage service
systems.scenario: Design a cloud file service that syncs large files across devices and supports sharing.
guide: Separate file metadata from blob storage and define chunking and resumable upload.
Cover sync protocol, versioning, and concurrent edit conflicts.
Discuss sharing permissions, encryption, and link revocation.
Address durability, replication, quotas, and recovery.

systems.title: Design a metrics platform
systems.scenario: Design an internal metrics platform ingesting millions of data points per second.
guide: Clarify query patterns, freshness, retention, and cardinality limits.
Design buffered ingestion and a time-series storage layout.
Cover downsampling, aggregation, alerting, and backpressure.
Define isolation, cost controls, and service-level objectives.

systems.title: Design a job scheduler
systems.scenario: Design a distributed scheduler that runs millions of delayed and recurring jobs.
guide: Define timing precision, recurring job semantics, and delivery guarantees.
Discuss sharding, safely claiming jobs, and worker coordination.
Cover retries, dead letters, fairness, and hot partitions.
Address clock issues, observability, and operational recovery.

systems.title: Design a real-time chat service
systems.scenario: Design one-to-one and group messaging for 100M users, including offline delivery and multi-device sync.
guide: Clarify delivery semantics, group sizes, ordering, retention, and online presence.
Define APIs for sending messages, syncing history, and acknowledging delivery.
Model conversations, memberships, messages, and per-device cursors.
Use persistent connections to gateways, a durable message log, and fanout workers.
Discuss ordering per conversation, retries, idempotency, offline queues, and regional failover.

systems.title: Design a video streaming platform
systems.scenario: Design a platform where creators upload videos and viewers stream them globally at multiple resolutions.
guide: Clarify upload size, playback startup target, peak viewers, and content privacy.
Separate the control plane (metadata) from the media data plane.
Upload directly to object storage with resumable multipart sessions.
Transcode asynchronously into adaptive bitrate segments and publish when ready.
Deliver segments through a CDN; cover access control, hot content, and processing retries.

systems.title: Design a ride-sharing service
systems.scenario: Design rider-driver matching with live locations, trip state, pricing, and payments.
guide: Clarify launch geography, location freshness, matching latency, and dispatch fairness.
Define rider request and driver availability APIs plus trip state transitions.
Partition driver locations by geographic cells and expire stale positions.
Search nearby cells, rank eligible drivers, and use an atomic offer/accept flow.
Discuss surge, duplicate requests, trip updates, payment idempotency, and safety.

systems.title: Design search autocomplete
systems.scenario: Design low-latency query suggestions that update as users type and support popular and personalized results.
guide: Clarify latency, languages, freshness, personalization, and privacy requirements.
Build a prefix index from normalized query and document signals.
Precompute top suggestions for common prefixes; use a trie or finite-state index.
Serve from a regional cache and rank candidates by popularity and context.
Stream anonymized usage events into offline aggregation and index refresh.

systems.title: Design a cloud file storage service
systems.scenario: Design a drive for file upload, sync, sharing, version history, and global downloads.
guide: Clarify file size, sync guarantees, sharing permissions, and version retention.
Separate file metadata and permissions from binary blob storage.
Use resumable chunked upload and content hashes for integrity/deduplication.
Propagate change events to sync clients with cursors and notification channels.
Discuss ACL checks, versioning, deletion recovery, and CDN delivery.

systems.title: Design a web crawler
systems.scenario: Design a polite crawler that discovers and indexes billions of pages while avoiding duplicate work.
guide: Clarify crawl freshness, supported content, politeness, and indexing scope.
Maintain a deduplicated frontier partitioned by host and priority.
Fetch through workers with per-host rate limits and robots policy checks.
Normalize URLs, fingerprint content, and schedule recrawls by change likelihood.
Discuss retries, traps, malicious content, and pipeline observability.

systems.title: Design a collaborative document editor
systems.scenario: Design a document editor with real-time multi-user editing, comments, and offline reconnection.
guide: Clarify document size, concurrent editors, offline behavior, and conflict expectations.
Choose an operation transformation or CRDT approach and define its tradeoffs.
Persist an ordered operation log and periodically compact snapshots.
Broadcast updates over persistent connections and authorize document membership.
Handle reconnect cursors, duplicate operations, presence, and version history.

systems.title: Design a distributed cache
systems.scenario: Design a cache tier for high read throughput, bounded latency, and predictable behavior during failures.
guide: Clarify cacheable data, consistency, eviction, TTL, and acceptable stale reads.
Choose key partitioning and replication strategy.
Define get/set/invalidate behavior and protect against cache stampedes.
Plan memory eviction, hot-key mitigation, and rolling resharding.
Discuss cache outage fallback, overload protection, and hit-rate observability.

systems.title: Design an event ticketing platform
systems.scenario: Design ticket discovery and checkout for a major event where demand spikes far above available inventory.
guide: Clarify inventory guarantees, queue fairness, payment timing, and cancellation policy.
Separate browsing and search from authoritative inventory reservation.
Use a virtual waiting room to control admission and shed overload.
Reserve inventory with atomic holds and expiry before payment confirmation.
Discuss idempotency, fraud, retries, and reconciliation of payment and inventory.

systems.title: Design a webhook delivery platform
systems.scenario: Design a multi-tenant webhook platform for 5 million customer accounts and up to 1 billion events per day. Customers register HTTPS endpoints and event subscriptions. Deliveries should be low-latency during normal operation, retried for up to 72 hours, observable, and protected from one tenant or failing endpoint overwhelming others. Assume at-least-once delivery is acceptable.
guide: Clarify event volume, fan-out, latency SLO, retry window, payload limits, endpoint security, and whether ordering is required per endpoint.

Estimate scale: 1B events/day is about 11.6K events/s average; with 10× peaks that is about 116K events/s. At five destinations per event, delivery averages about 58K requests/s and peaks near 580K/s. At 1 KB per event, the raw event stream is about 1 TB/day before replication.

Define APIs and data: event ingestion with an idempotency key, endpoint and subscription management, delivery status lookup, and replay. Model tenants, endpoints, subscriptions, immutable events, and delivery attempts.
Draw the flow: authenticated ingestion → durable event log → subscription fan-out → fair per-endpoint queues → delivery workers → customer endpoint; persist attempts and status.
Deep-dive on retries, exponential backoff with jitter, dead-lettering, replay, signature verification, tenant fairness, endpoint timeouts, and per-destination concurrency limits.

Explain tradeoffs: at-least-once means duplicates, so stable delivery IDs and receiver idempotency matter; strict ordering reduces parallelism; partition by endpoint when per-endpoint order is required.

systems.title: Design a payment processing platform
systems.scenario: Design a multi-region payment service for online merchants. Merchants create payment intents, customers confirm card payments, and merchants can capture, refund, and query transactions. Assume about 50 million payment attempts per day with peaks near 10,000 requests per second. The system must avoid duplicate charges, retain an auditable financial record, and recover safely when an external payment provider times out or returns delayed updates.
guide: Clarify authorization versus capture, partial capture/refund, supported payment methods, latency targets, availability, and merchant-visible states.

Estimate average volume: 50M attempts/day is about 580 per second; design for the stated 10K peak. If each persisted request/event averages 2 KB, peak raw ingress is about 20 MB/s before replication and provider callbacks.
Define merchant APIs and entities: payment intent, idempotency key, provider attempt, append-only ledger entry, and reconciliation record.
Draw the request path from authenticated API to idempotency check, durable state machine, transactional outbox, queue, provider connector, callback intake, and ledger posting.
Deep-dive on ambiguous timeouts, duplicate requests, asynchronous callbacks, ledger atomicity, provider outages, reconciliation, tokenization, and data retention.

Explain the delivery guarantee and tradeoffs: asynchronous processing improves resilience, but status may be pending; provider calls cannot share an atomic transaction with the local database, so idempotency and reconciliation are essential.

systems.title: Design a feature flag and remote configuration platform
systems.scenario: Design a multi-tenant feature flag service used by web and mobile applications. Teams create flags, define rules by user attributes or percentage rollout, and evaluate flags in SDKs or through a server API. Support 100,000 customer applications and up to 2 million evaluations per second globally. Most evaluation must remain local and finish in under 5 ms; a kill switch should reach active clients quickly. Config changes need auditability, tenant isolation, and safe behavior during network or control-plane outages.
guide: Clarify flag types, targeting operators, user identity, environments, SDK languages, evaluation placement, kill-switch propagation target, audit retention, and what clients should do with stale configuration.

Estimate which work is on the hot path: 2M evaluations/s globally is too expensive for a synchronous central service, so push signed configuration snapshots to regional edge endpoints and evaluate in SDK memory. Estimate control-plane writes separately; assume configuration changes are rare compared with evaluations.

Define APIs such as POST /v1/flags, PATCH /v1/flags/{key}, POST /v1/flags/{key}/rules, GET /v1/config/{environment}, and POST /v1/evaluate for server-side use. Model Flag, Rule, Segment, Environment, ConfigVersion, and AuditEvent with tenant and environment keys.

Draw the control plane from authenticated admin API to relational metadata store, transactional outbox, validation/compiler, and durable change stream. Draw the data plane from regional distribution endpoints to SDK caches that evaluate locally.
Deep-dive on percentage rollout stability, rule ordering, cache invalidation, mobile clients that sleep, kill-switch propagation, stale config, tenant boundaries, and configuration rollback.

Discuss consistency and resilience tradeoffs: asynchronous fanout gives fast local reads and tolerates network partitions, but propagation is not instantaneous. Versioned snapshots, expiry, acknowledgements, and visible propagation status make that limitation measurable.

systems.title: Design a durable message broker
systems.scenario: Design a multi-tenant message broker for backend services. Producers append events to named topics; independent consumer groups read and replay events. Support 200,000 events per second on average, 1 million at peak, 1 KB average payload, and seven days of retention. Preserve ordering within a partition, survive one broker failure without losing acknowledged events, and let a slow consumer recover without blocking producers indefinitely. Clarify whether transactions across partitions are required; exclude them in the initial design.
guide: Define publish acknowledgement, replay, retention, group consumption, per-partition ordering, availability and durability targets, and tenant quotas. Distinguish consumer delivery from the business side effects a consumer performs.

Use capacity math to motivate partitioning: 200K × 1 KB ≈ 200 MB/s and about 121 TB for seven days before replicas, indexes, and compression; three replicas need about 363 TB. Peak raw ingress is about 1 GB/s. Size disk and network capacity from benchmarks, including recovery headroom.

Specify CreateTopic, Produce(topic, key, producer_id, sequence, payload), Fetch(topic, partition, offset), and CommitOffset(group, partition, next_offset). Identify topic, partition, record, replica assignment, producer sequence, consumer group, and committed offset.

Trace the write path from metadata lookup to partition leader, local log append, follower replication, and durable acknowledgement. Trace reads from committed log offsets into consumer processing and offset commits.
Deep-dive on leader failover and fencing, producer retries, consumer rebalancing, poison events, retention versus lag, hot partitions, backpressure, and replay after crashes.

Compare per-partition ordering with global ordering, quorum durability with write latency, and at-least-once delivery with idempotent side effects. Explain why offset commits alone cannot guarantee exactly-once effects in an external database.

systems.title: Design a distributed tracing platform
systems.scenario: Design a multi-tenant tracing platform for microservices. SDKs emit spans with trace IDs, parent IDs, timings, and attributes. Engineers must retrieve a trace by ID and search recent slow or failed requests by service and time. Ingest 2 million spans per second at peak, averaging 500 bytes per span, and retain selected traces for seven days. Show accepted spans within 30 seconds and aim to retain all error traces that reach the sampling collectors. SDK overhead must stay bounded, and telemetry outages must not stall production requests.
guide: Clarify context propagation, trace lookup, search filters, retention, ingestion durability, tenant isolation, and the difference between spans never emitted and spans dropped after arrival. Define lateness and sampling limits explicitly.

At peak, 2M × 500 bytes ≈ 1 GB/s. If sustained, that is 86.4 TB/day and 604.8 TB over seven days before replication and indexes. A 5% byte retention rate would reduce payload storage to about 30.2 TB; error-biased sampling can exceed that estimate.

Define ExportSpans(batch), GET /v1/traces/{id}, and GET /v1/traces?service=&status=&min_duration=&start=&end=. Model tenant, trace ID, span ID, parent span ID, timestamps, attributes, and sampling decision.

Draw SDK → local collector → authenticated ingest → partitioned durable stream → trace assembler and sampler → object storage plus search index. Route all spans for a tenant/trace to one sampling owner.
Deep-dive on late spans, incomplete traces, tail-sampling memory, retries and duplicate spans, clock skew, attribute cardinality, and backpressure during outages.
Compare head versus tail sampling, completeness versus bounded waiting, indexed search versus payload storage cost, and fail-open SDK behavior versus a lossless telemetry promise.

systems.title: Design a real-time game leaderboard
systems.scenario: Design a global leaderboard for a multiplayer game with 50 million players per season. Trusted game servers submit score changes; players view the top 100, their own exact rank, and nearby competitors. Support 100,000 score updates and 200,000 leaderboard reads per second at peak. Updated scores should normally appear within two seconds. Scores are integers in [0,1000000]; higher scores rank first, ties use ascending player ID. Preserve accepted updates through a node failure and finalize an immutable leaderboard at season close.
guide: Clarify cumulative versus replacement scores, allowed decreases, tie rules, season boundaries, trusted score sources, rank freshness, and whether each page must reflect a single consistent snapshot.

A 50M-player season with 64 bytes per minimal player record needs about 3.2 GB raw, before indexes, object overhead, replication and history. At 100K updates/s and 200 bytes/event, peak event ingress is about 20 MB/s. Benchmark the ranked structure under contention rather than assuming raw size proves one node is enough.

Define SubmitScore(season, player, event_id, delta), GET /leaderboards/{season}/top, GET /leaderboards/{season}/players/{id}/rank, and GET /leaderboards/{season}/players/{id}/neighbors. Model accepted event, player score/version, ordered score entry, season state, and snapshot version.

Trace authenticated submission through deduplication and durable commit into ranked views. Start with one ordered index per leaderboard, then explain score-range partitioning and global rank calculation when throughput exceeds one owner.
Deep-dive on concurrent updates and score decreases, exact tie ordering, consistent counts, hot score ranges, duplicated events, cross-shard moves, caches, and season-close barriers.
Compare a simple single-owner sorted index with a coordinated sharded index. Distinguish exact rank at a committed snapshot from approximate counters assembled at different moments.

systems.title: Design a distributed lock and lease service
systems.tag: Leases, fencing tokens, and stale clients
systems.scenario: Design a coordination service that grants exclusive leases for named resources to backend workers. Support acquire, renew, release, and bounded waiting for a lease. Expect one million active resource names and 100,000 total coordination operations per second at peak. Workers can pause or lose connectivity at any time; the service must recover from one node failure without issuing conflicting committed ownership grants. Protected storage must reject stale owners after a newer owner is admitted. Start with independent resource locks and exclude atomic acquisition of multiple resources.
guide: Define ownership versus permission to mutate the downstream resource, lease duration, fairness, retry semantics, renewal deadlines, latency targets, and which external systems can enforce fencing tokens.

One million active leases at 200 bytes each is roughly 200 MB raw before indexes, log history, replicas, and deduplication. With 30-second leases renewed every 10 seconds, renewals alone can consume 100K operations/s; negotiate a higher budget, fewer renewable leases, or longer leases before claiming the stated throughput suffices.

Specify Acquire(resource, owner, request_id, ttl), Renew(lease_id, generation, request_id), Release(lease_id, generation), and Watch(resource, revision). Model current grant, immutable lease identity, expiry state, per-resource generation, and deduplicated request outcome.

Draw clients → shard router → consensus-backed resource shard → replicated lease state and expiration scheduler. Protected writes carry fencing tokens to a downstream store that atomically checks them.
Deep-dive on lost acknowledgements, delayed renewals, paused owners, leader failover, clock assumptions, watch races, retry storms, and compare-and-delete release.

Compare availability with exclusive grants during partitions, short leases with renewal cost, and advisory locks with enforceable fencing. Explain why an expired lease cannot physically stop a paused worker from resuming.

systems.title: Design a software package registry
systems.scenario: Design a registry for public and private software packages. Maintainers publish immutable package versions with dependency manifests, clients resolve version metadata and download artifacts, and administrators can quarantine compromised releases. Support 10 million stored versions, 1 million new versions per day, 5 MB average compressed artifact size, and peak 100,000 metadata reads plus 20,000 artifact downloads per second globally. Make acknowledged published versions durable and normally visible within 30 seconds. Specify what clients can expect when a cached or already downloaded release is revoked.
guide: Clarify namespace ownership, immutable version rules, mutable tags such as latest, supported version-range semantics, lockfiles, private access, provenance, quarantine and deletion policies.

Ten million versions at 5 MB need about 50 TB raw; 1M new versions/day adds about 5 TB/day before replicas. Peak artifact egress at 20K/s is about 100 GB/s, motivating a CDN. Treat metadata QPS and artifact bandwidth as separate scaling problems.

Define upload sessions, finalize-publish, package/version metadata lookup, conditional tag updates, artifact download, and quarantine APIs. Model namespace, package, version, digest-addressed blob, dependency manifest, tag revision, and audit record.

Trace authenticated publication through staging upload, checksum verification, validation/scanning, immutable blob storage and an atomic metadata commit. Trace installation through cached metadata, lockfile resolution, authorization, and CDN or object storage download.

Deep-dive on simultaneous publication, retry idempotency, metadata/blob consistency, dependency confusion, digest checks, private-cache isolation, compromised maintainers, quarantine propagation and orphan cleanup.

Compare immutable cacheable artifacts with mutable metadata, availability with immediate revocation, and client-side dependency resolution with a server resolver that must reproduce a particular metadata snapshot.

systems.title: Design a secrets management service
systems.scenario: Design a multi-tenant secrets service for production applications. Authorized workloads read versioned credentials, operators create and rotate secrets, and administrators revoke access with an audit trail. Support 10 million secret versions averaging 2 KB and 100,000 reads per second at peak across regions. Target under 100 ms regional read latency and durable acknowledged writes. Define a maximum 60-second policy revocation window for online reads, and explain what happens to credentials or secret bytes already delivered to a workload.
guide: Clarify static secret versions versus dynamically issued credentials, workload authentication, access policies, rotation schedules, version aliases, deletion recovery, audit requirements, and revocation scope.

Ten million versions at 2 KB require about 20 GB of plaintext-equivalent payload before encryption metadata, replicas and history. Peak read payload is about 200 MB/s. At 500 bytes per read audit event, 100K reads/s sustained produces about 4.32 TB/day of raw audit data.

Define CreateVersion(secret, value, request_id), ReadSecret(secret, version_or_alias), Rotate(secret), UpdatePolicy and Revoke. Model secret metadata, encrypted version, wrapped data key, policy revision, alias revision, workload identity and audit event.

Draw workload identity exchange → authenticated gateway → policy evaluation → ciphertext store/cache → key-management decrypt → authorized response. Separate administrative mutations, audit storage and rotation workers.

Deep-dive on envelope encryption, tenant isolation, authorization caching, rotation across external systems, concurrent rotations, key-service outages, audit durability and credentials retained by clients.

Compare plaintext caching with decryption cost, strict online revocation with outage availability, and static secrets with short-lived dynamic credentials. Make clear that revoking read permission does not erase an already disclosed password.

systems.title: Design a document search engine
systems.scenario: Design a multi-tenant full-text search service for company documents. Clients ingest, update and delete documents, then search terms and phrases with filters and ranked results. Store one billion documents averaging 5 KB, accept 50,000 document updates/s at peak, and serve 20,000 queries/s with a 300 ms p95 target. Normal updates should be searchable within 30 seconds. Documents have access controls, and permission removal must prevent further disclosure even if the search index has not yet refreshed.
guide: Clarify supported query syntax, ranking, phrase matching, filter fields, tenant sizes, deletion guarantees, pagination and access-control freshness. Keep prefix autocomplete outside the initial scope.

One billion 5 KB documents require about 5 TB of raw text. At 50K updates/s, peak source ingress is roughly 250 MB/s. Index expansion, stored positions, replicas and merge headroom determine actual disk demand; benchmark representative queries to size fanout and replicas.

Define PUT /documents/{id} with an idempotency key and version, DELETE /documents/{id}, GET /documents/{id}, and POST /search with query, filters, cursor and page size. Model authoritative document/version, change event, tombstone, postings, term positions and ACL revision.

Draw document API → authoritative store plus transactional outbox → stream → analyzer/index workers → immutable index segments and replicas. Query coordinators route to shards, intersect postings, rank local candidates and merge global results.
Deep-dive on out-of-order updates, segment refresh/merge, phrase positions, hot tenants, relevance statistics, permission checks before snippets, deletion tombstones and stable pagination.
Compare document sharding with term sharding, freshness with indexing throughput, exact top K with bounded-time partial results, and stale search candidates with authoritative permission enforcement.

systems.title: Design a content delivery network
systems.scenario: Design a multi-tenant CDN for immutable assets and mutable public web content. Customers configure an origin, cache rules, TLS domains and purge requests. Serve 1 million HTTP requests/s globally at peak with an average 100 KB cacheable response, targeting under 50 ms p95 edge processing time for cache hits, excluding client network transit. Aim for a 95% request hit ratio, bounded origin load during popular-object expiry, and purge propagation to active serving edges within 60 seconds. Define behavior during regional outages and for private or personalized responses.
guide: Clarify supported HTTP methods, response-size limits, cache eligibility, mutable versus versioned URLs, private content, custom domains, range requests, stale serving and the exact purge acknowledgement contract.

At 1M requests/s and 100 KB responses, edge delivery is roughly 100 GB/s. A 95% request hit ratio leaves about 50K origin fetches/s, but byte savings depend on which objects miss. Estimate hot working set per region and shield hit rates before choosing cache capacity.

Define customer configuration APIs, POST /purges with idempotency keys, purge-status lookup, and ordinary HTTP delivery. Model tenant/domain routing, origin policy, canonical cache key, cached object metadata, policy revision and purge generation.
Draw client → traffic steering → edge TLS/auth/cache → regional shield → origin. Separate the replicated control plane from the edge data plane and trace a cold miss, a fresh hit and a revalidation.

Deep-dive on cache keys and Vary, stampede suppression, cache poisoning, authorization before hits, purge races with in-flight fills, origin failure, stale responses and routing away from lagging edges.

Compare anycast versus DNS steering, eager replication versus pull caching, TTLs versus invalidation, and bounded purge guarantees versus offline-edge availability. Explain that purging a CDN cannot recall a client’s downloaded bytes.

systems.title: Design a distributed SQL analytics service
systems.tag: Snapshot reads, shuffles, and workload isolation
systems.scenario: Build a service where analysts submit read-only SQL against 10 PB of existing columnar tables in object storage. Support filters, joins, grouped totals, query status, and paged results. Up to 200 admitted queries can run concurrently. Aim for a 30-second p95 response for approved dashboard query shapes and allow longer batch runs. A query must use a consistent table snapshot even as new files arrive. A worker failure should be recoverable without duplicating result rows.
guide: Clarify read-only SQL features, consistency across tables, interactive versus batch latency, result expiry, tenant quotas, and cancellation.

A dashboard scan that reads 40 GB after pruning needs 1.3 GB/s just to scan within 30 seconds. If 200 such scans overlapped, they would need about 267 GB/s before shuffle, planning, or result delivery. Use measured scan rates and query mix to choose admission limits.
Sketch query submission, status, cancel, and paged results. Identify job ID, owner, query plan, snapshot IDs, stage attempts, and result manifest.
Draw a coordinator producing a plan, workers reading file splits, a shuffle exchanging groups or join keys, and a final stage publishing results.
Discuss partition pruning, join choice, hot keys, memory spill, worker or coordinator failure, and authorization when reading saved results.
Compare skipping queues to favor latency versus enforcing resource limits, and transient data exchange versus durable exchange for retries.

systems.title: Design an A/B experiment analysis platform
systems.scenario: Build an internal platform that reports whether product experiments changed conversion. Clients already have a feature delivery system. Your platform must record which randomized users were assigned and exposed, join outcome events to the correct cohort, show provisional results within 15 minutes, and publish a reproducible final report after a preset analysis window. Expect 20,000 events per second on average, a peak of 100,000 per second, 350 bytes per event, and 30 days of raw replay. Retried, late, or missing events must not silently bias the results.
guide: Clarify the randomization unit, what counts as enrollment and exposure, the outcome window, and what interim monitoring may conclude.
At 20,000 events/s and 350 bytes/event, budget about 7 MB/s on average and 35 MB/s at peak. Thirty days of raw replay is about 18 TB before replication or compression.
Define experiment creation, batch event ingestion, status, and report reads. Identify the experiment version, assignment record, exposure record, metric event, and report revision.
Draw ingest, durable events, per-user attribution, metric aggregation, data quality checks, and the results store. Keep assignment and exposure counts visible separately.
Explain duplicate handling, out-of-order joins, uneven loss across variants, configuration changes, and late data after finalization.
Discuss provisional streaming versus exact batch reconciliation, confidence intervals, and safe handling of repeated looks at the data.

systems.title: Design a nearby place search service
systems.tag: Radius filtering, relevance, and spatial sharding
systems.scenario: Build a service where people search for places near a location using a required radius and optional text or category filters. Return ranked places, distance, and opening status. Owners can change listings, and updates should appear in search within a minute. Assume 100 million listings, 50,000 peak searches per second, and 2,000 peak listing updates per second. Aim for p95 under 150 ms for searches up to 10 km. Explain how you avoid missing matches near a city or shard boundary.
guide: Clarify whether the radius is straight-line or travel distance, how text and distance influence rank, and when to evaluate opening hours.

Estimate 100 GB of raw searchable listing data at 1 KB per listing, plus index structures and replicas. At 50,000 searches/s and four visited shards per search, budget about 200,000 shard requests/s before retries.

trend.title: Calibrate offline agent scores against what users experience
trend.intro: Offline evaluations can catch regressions before users see a change. To use a score for release decisions, first learn how well it predicts the outcome you care about in production. For a support agent, compare changes in offline task success with changes in correctly resolved cases.

points.title: Pair comparable offline and online results
points.text: For past prompt changes, log the offline score change and the measured A/B effect on a chosen outcome. Analyze prompt edits separately from model or tool changes if those change how the score relates to the outcome.

points.title: Use scores to decide which changes need an experiment
points.text: While you are still learning the relationship, use an offline score to catch clear breakage and require an online test for meaningful rollout decisions. After local validation, use the estimated uncertainty to decide which low-risk changes a score can support and which still need an A/B test.

points.title: Audit after adopting a faster release path
points.text: Randomly send some changes from the faster path through a normal experiment. Compare observed outcomes with what the offline scores predicted. Recalibrate after a change in model, judge, or traffic mix, especially when a judge might favor one model’s answers.

trendHistory.title: Let agents investigate incidents with read-only access
trendHistory.intro: Use an agent to assemble incident evidence and prepare a handoff for the on-call engineer. For example, it can compare when checkout errors started with when a deployment rolled out and show the traces behind its hypothesis. The incident process still owns the change decision.

points.title: Start with a scoped evidence account
points.text: Give the investigator access to the affected service’s health metrics, selected logs and deployment history. Ask it to link the evidence for each hypothesis and say what observation would rule it out.

points.title: Make the handoff reviewable
points.text: Have the investigator record the affected service, supporting observations, a proposed change, and how the operator would check recovery. Enforce any write permissions and approval checks at the tool boundary.

points.title: Agree on recovery signals
points.text: Before a change, pick a trusted signal and time window. For checkout, the on-call engineer might watch completion rate and p95 latency against the pre-incident baseline. Rehearse on past incidents and measure useful findings and incorrect escalations.

trendHistory.title: Test what an agent actually changed
trendHistory.intro: A useful agent evaluation checks two things. Did the task succeed in the system, and did the agent get there through an acceptable sequence of actions? Start with an outcome you can inspect, then use the trace to understand failures.

points.title: Verify the outcome directly
points.text: For an agent that books a meeting, inspect the test calendar for one event with the right time and invitees. Also test a retry and check that it does not create a duplicate.

points.title: Use the trace to diagnose failures
points.text: If the event is missing or wrong, inspect the tool inputs and responses. That can tell you whether the agent misread the request, used the wrong calendar, or ignored a conflict.

points.title: Turn a failed run into a repeatable check
points.text: Save a scrubbed or synthetic example with the starting calendar and expected end state. Rerun it after changing instructions, tools, or the model. Track passing cases, latency, and cost so a fix has visible tradeoffs.
